passages.text: We truly tell you that on the day of judgment it will be more bearable for the land of Sodom and Gomorrah than for you to remain in the place of disobedience. First, because you did not understand what is reasonable for yourselves; second, because, after hearing about us, you did not come to us; third, because you disobeyed us even when we came. Therefore, out of concern for you, we freely pray that our peace may come upon you. If you wish to have it, you must eagerly undertake not to do wrong and courageously bear being wronged. Human nature would not endure this unless it first gained knowledge of the surpassing benefit, which is to know the righteous nature of the one who surpasses everything: that, in avenging the wronged, he punishes, and that he benefits the reverent forever.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἢ τῷ τῆς ἀπειθείας τόπῳ ἐνδιατελεῖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: than for you to remain in the place of disobedience
lexical_decisions.rationale: The infinitive is read as remaining in the location designated by the dative, with the addressed listeners as its contextual subject. A rendering that treats the place itself as the object of judgment is also possible, but must still account for the expressed remaining infinitive rather than omit it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in avenging the wronged, he punishes
lexical_decisions.rationale: The wronged are the object of the avenging participle. The finite verb's punished object is unexpressed; the main text does not make the wronged people the ones punished, and leaves the implied wrongdoers unnamed.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the reverent
lexical_decisions.rationale: The term describes those practicing reverence or piety, with the divine referent supplied by the surrounding argument. It is not replaced by a denominational group name.

passages.text: Oh, God's great, wise hand, which does everything in all things! For he has brought into being a countless multitude of birds, a varied multitude in which each differs from another in every respect: colors, beaks, claws, looks, dispositions, sounds, and everything else. How many different forms of plants there are too, distinguished by countless colors, qualities, and scents! How many animals of the dry land and of the waters, whose shapes, forms, arrangements, colors, ways of life, dispositions, natures, and multitude cannot be recounted! And also the multitudes and heights of mountains, differences among stones, fearsome recesses, springs, rivers, lakes, seas, harbors, islands, forests, the whole inhabited world, and uninhabited places.

lexical_decisions.chosen: dispositions
lexical_decisions.rationale: The same word is rendered consistently in the bird and animal lists. Opinions or judgments are lexical alternatives, but dispositions better describes the behavioral character attributed to these living creatures without removing their cognitive individuality.

lexical_decisions.chosen: looks
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun can mean the eyes' looks or expressions, or the act of looking. Looks preserves that range rather than specifying eye color or anatomical structure not named here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: arrangements
lexical_decisions.rationale: The word can indicate placements, positions, or bodily arrangements. It is distinguished from the adjacent shapes and forms rather than collapsed into them.

passages.text: Thus Adam, made according to his likeness, is created blind, is handed over without knowledge of good or evil, is found a transgressor, is expelled from the garden, and is punished with death. Likewise, the one who fashioned him, since he does not see from every direction, says concerning Sodom's destruction, ‘Come, let us go down and see whether they are carrying things through according to the outcry from them that comes to me; if not, so that I may know.’ He thereby shows himself ignorant. As for saying about Adam, ‘Let us cast him out, lest he stretch out his hand, touch the tree of life, eat, and live forever,’ saying ‘lest’ shows ignorance; adding ‘lest he eat and live forever’ also shows envy. And the writing, ‘God reflected that he had made the human,’ shows both reconsideration and ignorance. For ‘reflected’ is deliberation, by which someone, through ignorance, wishes to determine precisely the outcome of what he wants, or the reflection of one regretting what did not turn out as intended. And the writing, ‘The Lord smelled a fragrant scent,’ belongs to one in need, while taking pleasure in the smoke from flesh does not belong to a good one. Testing too, as it is written, ‘The Lord tested Abraham,’ belongs to an evil one ignorant of the outcome of endurance.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: γνῶσιν ἀγαθοῦ ἢ κακοῦ οὐκ ἔχων παραδέδοται
lexical_decisions.chosen: is handed over without knowledge of good or evil
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive handed over and the absence of knowledge are both retained. The clause does not name the recipient or purpose of the handing over, so none is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ κατὰ τὴν κραυγὴν αὐτῶν τὴν ἐρχομένην πρὸς μὲ συντελοῦνται
lexical_decisions.chosen: whether they are carrying things through according to the outcry from them that comes to me
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied verb concerns completion or carrying through, but does not expressly name the conduct being completed. The English retains that open expression rather than supplying the familiar wording from a different form of the scriptural quotation.

lexical_decisions.chosen: shows both reconsideration and ignorance
lexical_decisions.rationale: In the argument about God's reflected decision, metanoeo concerns reconsideration, not a moral-spiritual redirection toward God. The policy's contextual exception is therefore applied; the source's polemical accusation is retained without imposing a doctrine that resolves it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the smoke from flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: The noun denotes the fatty smoke or smell associated with flesh being cooked or offered. The main text retains flesh and smoke without identifying a particular animal or adding a sacrificial procedure.

passages.text: In this way Simon seemed to show many things from the scriptures: that God is subject to every passion. Peter replied, ‘If an evil and thoroughly wicked person takes no pleasure in exposing himself for the things in which he sins, answer me.’ Simon said, ‘He takes no pleasure in it.’ Peter said, ‘How, then, can God be evil and wicked, if through his remnant the evil things written publicly against him were added?’ Simon said, ‘It is possible that the accusation against him was written by another power contrary to his intention.’ Peter said, ‘Then let us investigate this first. If he exposed himself by his own will, as you already agreed, he is not wicked. But if it was by another power, we must investigate and examine with all our strength whether someone accused him, though he alone is good, of all the evils.’

lexical_decisions.chosen: through his remnant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied noun λείμμα denotes a remnant, remainder, or residue. His remnant is retained as a potentially collective agent rather than silently substituting a different noun meaning will or permission. Its exact referent is not established by this passage.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μή τις αὐτὸν μόνον ἀγαθὸν ὄντα ἐπὶ πᾶσιν τοῖς κακοῖς ὑπέβαλεν
lexical_decisions.chosen: whether someone accused him, though he alone is good, of all the evils
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can denote insinuating, falsely imputing, or bringing an accusation. The main reading preserves the possibility of another power's false charge and the explicit alone-good qualification without naming that power.

source_issues.issue: The printed remnant or residue noun is unusual in the argument about publicly written accusations. The English preserves its ordinary lexical meaning with the referent unresolved; it is not an emendation to an unprinted word for will. A collective remnant belonging to God is defensible, but that identification remains tentative.

passages.text: On the following day in Tyre, I came to the quiet place as we had agreed. I saw and greeted the others along with some additional people, but, not seeing Apion, I asked why he was absent. Someone said that he had been seriously unwell in body since the previous evening. When I said that it would be reasonable to set out at once and visit him, nearly everyone asked that I speak with them first; afterward I could visit him too. So, with everyone of one mind, I began to speak:

lexical_decisions.source_quote: δυσαρρώστως αὐτὸν ἀπ’ αὐτῆς ἑσπέρας ἐσχηκέναι τὸ σωμάτιον
lexical_decisions.chosen: he had been seriously unwell in body since the previous evening
lexical_decisions.rationale: The report concerns bodily illness. The diminutive body-form need not imply that Apion was small, weak, or a child; the English retains its bodily reference without adding a diagnosis.

passages.text: ‘After leaving here yesterday, friends, I confess that I could not sleep, so concerned was I about the inquiry that was to take place with Apion. While I lay awake, what I had contrived against him in Rome came rushing into my mind. It was as follows. From childhood I, Clement, loved truth and sought what mattered to the soul, spending my time on refutations and demonstrations but unable to find anything conclusive. Through brooding I drifted into illness. While I was lying sick, Apion came to Rome. He was a friend of my father's and stayed as my guest. On learning that I was bedridden, he came in to me, being not uninitiated in medicine, and asked the reason for my confinement to bed. But I, knowing that this man held the Jews in intense hatred, to the point of writing many books against them, and that even now he welcomed Simon into friendship not from love of learning, but because he knew him to be a Samaritan who hated Jews and had come forward against them—for this reason he had drawn Simon close, so that he might learn something from him against the Jews—’

lexical_decisions.chosen: on refutations and demonstrations
lexical_decisions.rationale: The paired terms concern dismantling and establishing arguments. Both sides of the inquiry are retained, rather than reducing the activity to criticism alone.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὑπὸ τῆς συνοίας ἐξώκειλα εἰς νόσον
lexical_decisions.chosen: Through brooding I drifted into illness
lexical_decisions.rationale: The mental preoccupation is connected with illness, and the movement verb retains a faint drifting or running-aground image. Dejection or anxious reflection are material alternatives to brooding; no medical diagnosis is inferred.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He was a friend of my father's
lexical_decisions.rationale: The inherited or paternal friendship is rendered through the father, not as a claim that Apion was Clement's biological father.

lexical_decisions.chosen: being not uninitiated in medicine
lexical_decisions.rationale: The litotes and initiation image are retained. The phrase indicates some medical knowledge without certifying professional qualification.

passages.text: ‘Knowing these things beforehand about Apion, as soon as he asked the cause of the illness, I answered in pretense, “I am suffering what young people suffer, and my soul is in pain.” He said, “My child, take courage and speak to me as to a father: what is your soul's illness?” I again sighed in pretense, as though ashamed to speak about love, and by my silence and downward nodding gave him the suspicion of what I wished to suggest. Truly persuaded that I was in love with a woman, he said, “There is nothing in life for which help cannot be found. For when I was young, I too fell in love with a most distinguished woman. I thought not only that it was impossible to obtain her, but had no hope even of ever greeting her. Yet I met an Egyptian very thoroughly versed in the arts of magicians, became his friend, and disclosed my love. He not only put himself at my disposal for everything I wanted, but, showing still greater generosity toward me, did not begrudge teaching me the incantation through which I succeeded. Persuaded by the generosity of my teacher through his secret instruction, and having succeeded once, I ceased from love.”’

lexical_decisions.chosen: in pretense
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both occurrences make Clement's performance explicitly feigned. The translation does not present the supposed romantic illness as an authentic disclosure.

lexical_decisions.chosen: a most distinguished woman
lexical_decisions.rationale: The superlative concerns being worthy of regard or mention, not expressly physical beauty. Most remarkable is a material alternative; beautiful would add a characteristic not supplied here.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the incantation through which I succeeded
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source reports an incantation but does not provide its words or method in this passage. The English neither invents a spell nor claims independent efficacy.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having succeeded once, I ceased from love
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the single success and the ensuing cessation of love are retained. The statement is not rewritten into continued passion or an unexpressed permanent relationship.

passages.text: For just as fearsome snakes draw sparrows to themselves by their breath, so these beings draw those sharing their table toward their own will, mingling with their minds through food and drink. They transform themselves in dreams into the forms of carved images in order to increase deception. For the carved image is neither alive nor possessed of a divine spirit; the demon that appeared made use of its form. To how many other people have they similarly appeared in dreams, and, when those people met one another while awake and compared what they had seen in dreams, did not agree? Thus that is no longer a dream apparition, but is either a demon's appearance or the soul's, giving images in response to the fears and desire that arise. For, struck in mind by fear, it brings forth images through dreams. If you think that carved images, being possessed of breath, can perform such things, set them on a balance. With the beam level, place the counterweight on the other pan, and ask them to become either heavier or lighter. If that happens, they have breath. But it does not happen. If it does, is such a thing thereby a god? For this can happen even by a demon's finger. Worms move too, and are not called gods.

lexical_decisions.chosen: by their breath
lexical_decisions.rationale: The snake comparison uses breath or exhalation, not a separate snake spirit. The ensuing mingling of demons with minds is retained as the speaker's ancient explanatory claim.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ὥστε οὐκέτι ὄναρ ἐπιφανείη ἐκεῖνό ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Thus that is no longer a dream apparition
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual form ἐπιφανείη is taken nominally as apparition or manifestation alongside the copula ἐστιν. An optative verbal reading, might appear, is morphologically possible but does not fit this copular sequence readily. No divine adjective absent from the clause is supplied.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: εἰ δὲ ἔσται, οὕτω τὸ τοιοῦτο θεός ἐστιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: If it does, is such a thing thereby a god?
lexical_decisions.rationale: The following demon-finger and worm counterexamples support a rhetorical challenge rather than an affirmation of divinity. The Greek clause can formally be read as an assertion; the rhetorical-question punctuation is interpretive and disclosed, not a change to the words.

lexical_decisions.chosen: heavier or lighter
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two weight alternatives govern the balance test. No modern measurement, physical explanation, or successful experimental result is supplied.

source_issues.issue: The supplied form παρίᾳ has no defensible clear meaning or agreement established in this construction. The draft renders the surrounding fears, desire, and images but leaves this word's contribution unresolved; that is an incomplete rendering, not an emendation or a claim of full coverage. Source-level or scholarly resolution is required before publication.

passages.text: How many also falsely claim oracular responses and cures accomplished by these images, and confirm them with oaths? How many have hired themselves out, undertaking through certain contrivances to suffer something and proclaiming it in this way, then, having been restored from their affliction by a counteracting treatment, say that the cure was revealed by an oracle, so that they may label the unfeeling thing an object of worship? How many of these objects were consecrated from the beginning by magical art, so that they might give oracles? Yet over a long time these too proved discordant. How many now practice sorcery, wishing to strengthen such things? Nevertheless, if something has powers of divination or healing, that does not make it a god.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having been restored from their affliction by a counteracting treatment
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive restoration concerns the people in respect of their affliction; the affliction itself is not restored or strengthened. The counteraction opposes the contrived affliction. Its exact technique is not given, so no substance, remedy, or procedure is supplied.

lexical_decisions.chosen: so that they may label the unfeeling thing an object of worship
lexical_decisions.rationale: The insensate thing is the object labeled, with object of worship its assigned designation. The claim of an oracular cure is being used to confer that designation; the main text does not invent an actual written dedication.

lexical_decisions.chosen: over a long time these too proved discordant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The loss of agreement or reliability is retained without inventing a particular failed oracle or a quantitative error rate.

source_issues.issue: The supplied verb ὑνερπολῇ has no defensible lexical rendering established here. The draft translates the following giving of oracles but does not claim to have translated this first coordinated action. It has not silently substituted an unprinted form or invented a dotted gap. The unresolved word blocks publication until source-level or scholarly resolution.
